title: Deciding when it is done
blurb: The model stops thinking on its own. A small learned switch looks after each round and decides whether the thinking is finished. This part is built, but it has never been run.

scenes.heading: Where we are: the stop switch

caption.text: The model thinks in rounds, one lap at a time.
The stop switch decides when the thinking is finished.
It is built, but it has never been run.

scenes.heading: The problem: a fixed dial is a guess

caption.text: The older design had a dial: the same number of rounds for every question, set by hand (12 in the tested model, 8 in another).
Easy questions may need fewer rounds. Hard questions may need more.

scenes.heading: Too many rounds can cost points

caption.text: Older models were trained for 8 rounds. In a round-count test on two copies, the score on practice-like questions stopped rising at 8 rounds.
On all 8 copies we checked (those two and six more), running 16 rounds scored 0.8 to 1.9 points lower than 8 rounds.
So too few rounds hurt, and too many may hurt too.

scenes.heading: After each round, a small head says stop or go

caption.text: After every round, the stop switch, a small head, reads one of the thinker's note cards.
It gives a number from 0 to 1. At 0.5 or more, the thinking stops.
It always runs at least 1 round, and never more than 32.
The stop switch has 257 numbers when each card has 256, and 513 when each has 512.

scenes.heading: How it is taught: the settled label

caption.text: Training gives every round a label: stop, or keep going.
The label says stop when the answer is right now, or when no later round is right.
So the stop switch is also taught to stop on questions it cannot solve.

scenes.heading: The fix: count the label only in full batches

caption.text: Practice uses batches of questions, and some batches run only 8 rounds. There, a question first right at round 10 looks never right.
So the label says stop at round 1, and the stop switch would learn to stop too early.
Fix: the stop switch learns only from batches that run all 32 rounds, about 1 in 4.

scenes.heading: The risk: a stop that fires too early

caption.text: The label only sees the rounds a question actually ran.
So a stop that fires early may never be shown a later right answer (suggested).
The first run is planned to report how often questions stop early, and their answers. This is reported only, not a pass mark.

scenes.heading: How it will be judged: marks set in advance

caption.text: Key pass marks (bars the test must reach) were written before any run. They are targets, not results.
On average, 1-step questions must use at most half the rounds of the longest ones (code: 11 steps; plan: 12).
Always-32 is the same model forced to think all 32 rounds. Practised questions: within 1 point. Longer chains: within 2.
It fails if it never stops early (rounds within 10% of 32), or if longer chains fall over 5 below always-32.

scenes.heading: If it fails: no build switch removes the stop

caption.text: No build switch removes the stop. The switches cover things like Gemma and calls, not the stop.
A trained copy can still be run with the stop ignored and a forced number of rounds, as a test.
The nearest model with no stop is the outside-calculator model (T1SDR), with a fixed 8 rounds.
The stop has never run. Its first run is planned after the separate G1 size test finishes (not covered here).

scenes.heading: Fast and slow: one thinker, not two

caption.text: People talk about fast thinking and slow thinking. Few rounds is like the fast kind, many rounds like the slow kind.
We suggest one looped thinker gives both, so no separate fast and slow model is needed (suggested, not tested).
To remember: the stop switch decides, the limit is 32 rounds, and the stop is built but not yet run.
